Great patch, and I love this feature. I think the real work here to do, as you suggest, is getting implementer feedback on whether they're OK with these semantics. Probably TC39 would be a good place to broach the topic, since even though this is a web platform feature, most of the work in ensuring this consistency would happen in the JS engine, I think.

To be clear, the inconsistency you're worried about would only last for a single event loop turn, right?

@domenic Yes, should be just one turn, I think. Not so bad, but I imagine that languagechange's guarantees exist to avoid the same amount of badness.

I can talk to implementers and users at TC39 offline, but would this be considered in scope for a main committee presentation?

@littledan I'd be a little afraid some in TC39 would want to tie this to "Jobs" (which we haven't refactored yet and don't seem the right place), but it does somewhat affect how `Date` works so from that perspective it seems good to at least get aired.

I didn't realize that language change used similar verbiage, hmm. I wonder if it's even true in implementations :). I suppose it would be easier to implement than the corresponding one for times though.

I'd go for offline discussions with implementers at TC39, instead of a full presentation to the committee.
Do you mean timezone change, or offset change?

@rtm Good question. I mean time zone change. You can read the time zone from Intl, and the text here specifically calls out that case. Even if the offset for 'now' stays the same, offsets for past or future dates may change with a time zone change.The timezone is also represented with various formatting methods.
Removing security/privacy label since time zones (and changes to them) are already exposed to script. This doesn't really change anything.
This is a good idea. It doesn't expose any information that isn't already accessible, and would mean that applications wouldn't need to poll. Better for performance, better for battery life.

I'm not sure if we actually have to delay the timezone update until this callback runs. The delay will cause some additional implementation complexity, and I haven't heard anybody ask for it. I'm thinking to update this patch to remove that requirement.

Edit: Updated the patch to remove that aspect of it.

The W3C I18N WG [tasked](https://www.w3.org/International/track/actions/759) me with saying that we reviewed this proposal at our [TPAC meeting](https://www.w3.org/2018/10/22-i18n-minutes.html) with @littledan and that we support this proposal.
It's unclear how/whether WPT tests can be written for this feature. I filed https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/issues/13683 to ask for advice.

I still think it would be better if an agent cached the timezone and we only changed it from a task at the same time the event is dispatched, but I guess I can live with this. I don't think there's precedent for state and the corresponding event to not be synchronized.

Once we have multi-implementer support, let's poll the implementers to hear their thoughts on these alternatives.

FWIW, no one I've talked to about this feature who's not an HTML editor had any strong concerns, use cases or expectations in this area (and many were actually surprised by the idea that the timezone update would be delayed), though I can definitely see the case for this delay.

Note that JS implementations which implement https://github.com/tc39/ecma262/pull/778 will have some difficulty using OS APIs for timezone operations, so it's likely to not be as taxing to implement the delay on them as it would be on certain JS implementations which don't follow that patch.

I think we need to ask ourself the question- how will developer use this event? and why do they care about the change of timezone inside the JS code. And what kind of thing could the developer perform inside such event handler?
And then we need to ask, if that happen before the timezone in the system really change, would those code be able to get the necessary information to perform the desired tasks.

Currently, js code can find out the current timezone by 
```
(new Intl.DateTimeFormat()).resolvedOptions().timeZone
```
and the timeZone is updated by the system time zone even inside ICU
I think we can imaging if we allow the developer to register their ontimezonechange handler, they will likely to make the call to get the update timezone value from
 (new Intl.DateTimeFormat()).resolvedOptions().timeZone 
or reconstruct their Intl.DateTimeFormat object upon the change of the timezone.
So I believe the ontimezonechange event dispatcher should happen AFTER the internal state of Intl.DateTimeFormat got updated. Otherwise if the event handler call the Intl.DateTimeFormat it will get back the "soon to be changed" information and won't be able to get the "just-changed" information.
If there is a real need to track the event before the timezone change, then we probably should divided into two events
onbeforetimezonechange
and
onaftertimezonechange
But I personally do not believe there is a need for onbeforetimezonechange. Please educate me if you have some use cases for that I am not able to imaging.
I worry more about script being able to observe a different timezone before the event is dispatched. I don't think there's a need for two events.

There are some [privacy concerns](https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/forum/#!msg/blink-dev/4BUSE2aTQEc/a5-gBNTdCAAJ) discussed on the blink-dev I2P thread about this PR. We might want to address those with a mitigation in the specification itself, to ensure that it is maximally interoperable.

> @annevk  I still think it would be better if an agent cached the timezone and we only changed it from a task at the same time the event is dispatched, but I guess I can live with this. I don't think there's precedent for state and the corresponding event to not be synchronized.

Uncancellable change events like this often happen after, and are not coupled with the update. Ex. Scrolling, orientation change, online, offline, resize, media queries, etc. The spec queues an event and if polling you can observe the change sooner. It's not like the browser waits to issue any network requests until the online event is about to fire. :) With throttling in background tabs events are also often very delayed. 

I'm not sure in general "something changed" events have consistent or precise timing, most queue an event and there's a delta the size of the pending task list on the event loop. ex. Some are queued until paint time, which means in a background tab they never fire until being foregrounded, while the state itself is observable through polling long before that.

I think the "precedent for state and the corresponding event to not be synchronized" is all specs that say "queue an event".

Addressing privacy issues in the specification will reduce interoperability problems in the future. If the spec is entirely silent and some implementations fire events simultaneously in the background, sites could come to rely on that behavior and there would be interop disadvantages for implementations that wanted to mitigate the privacy risk. In general, I think we'll all benefit from building in and explicitly addressing mitigations during the spec design discussion, rather than trying to add mitigations later in each implementation and hoping they don't conflict with the spec or with interop of other implementations.

Immediately would mean that there's an atomic change, where no code can observe the timezone update before the event fires, and that event can observe the update. The "some time before" alternative is that the user agent *may* perform the update earlier, meaning that some code may run in the middle and observe the update before the event fires. Remember that this is all in a single-threaded environment, so there's no "racing". It's hard to write a test for this since the UA is allowed to implement the former semantics if the latter option is chosen.

If the two different behavior options could not be expressed by test as two "testable" specification options, (not necessary mutually exclusive expectation, for example we may have option A pass both tests and option B pass one of test would still be considered "testable", both test should be able to observe the change of the timezone, of course ) then I do not think it make sense for us to discuss them as TWO different options here, right?

Hi folks.

I (now) work on tracking preventing in Chrome.

The proposed TZ change event increases the [ephemeral fingerprinting](https://github.com/asankah/ephemeral-fingerprinting) risk because of the information carried in the time window during which a TZ change occurs. This increase in risk isn't expected to be that significant since the window length that would qualify as identifying is already large owing to the low frequency of TZ changes.

However, this means that JS observing a TZ change is already not good news for identity separation across browsing contexts. My reading of the text is that it doesn't preclude a UA from implementing mitigation strategies involving the presentation of the new TZ to JS execution contexts at different points in time.

Hence I have no objections to this proposal.

Hi folks,

Given that we don't have good data yet for how these time-zone change events
are distributed, it's difficult to recommend a good fuzzing strategy. I'd
suggest something like:

1. For the active top-level browsing context -- i.e. the one that has system
   input focus [1] -- the UA can dispatch the event immediately.

1. Same goes for top-level browsing contexts that are (schemeful) same-site
   with the active top-level browsing context. Given that these can be within
   the same cookie scope, we assume that they can already coordinate
   identities.

1. Where possible, delay the event until the page is activated. This should be
   trivial for pages that don't have active timers.

1. For pages that have active timers or are active in the background, dispatch
   the event with a fuzzed delay.
   
   There's insufficient data on the distribution of these events along the
   timeline in order to recommend a concrete fuzzing strategy. So the initial
   recommendation is to pick a random value from the uniform continuous
   distribution [0, 1hour).
   
   Two top-level browsing contexts that are mutually same-site and can access
   shared local state should use the same fuzz factor. Otherwise having
   multiple correlated time fuzzed events will allow the site to gather more
   information than a single fuzzed event.
   
   This delay is in addition to timer throttling that the UA employs. While the
   UA can "round up" the delay to a nearby activation time slot, it should avoid
   firing the event on more than one top-level site at a time.

Once more data is available and analyzed, we can propose a more concrete
recommendation for how to determine the fuzzed delay and the interaction with
fuzzed events and background throttling.

[1]: # "The concept of a system focused top-level browsing context is still not well defined yet."

I am not a WebDriver editor, but can give thoughts from the perspective of someone who has helped a few teams add WebDriver extensions for browser-testing purposes. We have historically encouraged spec authors to add the 'automation/testing support' section to the same specification as the feature that the automation is for. This helps keep the automation APIs 'in sync' with the feature APIs, and also keeps the main WebDriver spec leaner and clearer (rather than be a laundry list of extensions).

There is significant prior art here; permissions, reporting, sensors, webauthn, and background fetch all have webdriver extensions in their spec.
